title: New research shows how agentic voice AI is gaining autonomy in business
summary: 359 business leaders weigh in: 57% have deployed voice AI agents and 82% report positive ROI. See the new RingCentral and G2 research.
body_markdown:
Voice AI agents are taking on a larger role in business conversations. Fifty-seven percent of leaders surveyed have voice AI agents actively deployed, with another 10% piloting them. Among leaders with live deployments who were asked to rate returns, 82% report a positive ROI. As businesses put these capabilities into practice, they’re also determining how much responsibility to give agents and where human involvement is still required.


New research from RingCentral and G2 offers a closer look at how those decisions are playing out.[The Rise of Agentic Voice AI: From Conversations to Outcomes](https://www.ringcentral.com/report/2026-agentic-voice-ai-trends.html) examines how businesses are deploying, governing, and measuring agentic voice AI, including the level of autonomy agents have today and what businesses consider as they expand their role.


The research itself also put voice AI to work. In a first-of-its-kind study, G2’s voice AI agents conducted 359 in-depth interviews with business leaders across six industries, capturing more than 86 hours of conversations about their experiences with agentic voice AI.


## Voice AI is starting to prove its operational value


Voice brings AI directly into the moments when customers and employees need answers and action. That makes it a useful proving ground for agentic AI, as businesses can see what happens when agents move beyond providing information and begin taking on work within the conversation.


The research shows that the shift is already underway. Many businesses are starting with high-volume, repeatable interactions where the task and expected outcome are relatively clear, including customer support and service, scheduling, call routing and intake, reminders, and follow-ups.


Among the 82% reporting positive returns, businesses cited cost savings, time savings, and the ability to redirect employees to more complex work.


Voice is also generating information that businesses can use after an individual interaction ends. Sixty-two percent of leaders said their organizations use conversation data to inform decisions or improve processes, whether measuring service quality or feeding insights into analytics systems to track outcomes.


“AI has reached an inflection point. The question is no longer whether businesses will invest, but where those investments will deliver real returns,” said Jennifer Caukin, Group Vice President of Corporate Marketing at RingCentral. “Voice AI is emerging as one of the clearest answers because it sits where customer intent, action and business value converge. This research shows the market is crossing that threshold now, with businesses moving beyond pilots and putting voice AI to work with greater autonomy, measurable ROI and real operational impact.”


## Businesses are giving voice AI agents meaningful autonomy


As businesses see tangible results from voice AI, they’re also trusting agents with more work. Among 191 active deployments described in the study, 92% operate with high or partial autonomy. Forty-seven percent operate with high autonomy, with a human available when needed, while the other 45% operate with partial autonomy and structured escalation.


On average, voice AI agents handle 69% of an assigned task without human intervention, demonstrating how much responsibility businesses are already giving agents within defined workflows.


Greater autonomy also means businesses need clear conditions for when a person should step in. Sixty-two percent of escalation approaches analyzed involve handing work to a person when an agent encounters complexity, uncertainty, or a predefined trigger. Another 31% bring people in earlier for high-stakes, emotional, or judgment-heavy interactions.


With those boundaries in place, businesses are building a model of autonomy where agents resolve routine interactions independently, and humans take over when a conversation calls for their expertise.


## Greater autonomy puts more focus on the customer and brand experience


When a voice AI agent interacts directly with a customer, it represents the business in that moment. How it responds and moves the conversation forward can shape the customer’s experience with the brand.


Asked about their biggest concerns with agentic voice AI, 59% of leaders pointed to potential brand or customer harm. Privacy and governance followed at 24%, while 17% cited accuracy and reliability.


Businesses are pairing an AI agent’s performance metrics, like accuracy and resolution, with customer feedback and human review. Details within each interaction matter too, including how closely an agent follows required processes and how it handles a difficult conversation.


Those combined indicators show businesses where agents can act on their own and where additional oversight is valuable.


## High-stakes conversations are expanding the role of voice AI


Even some interactions once assumed to require a person are being reconsidered. Thirty-five percent of leaders said voice AI can be a better option than chat-based AI or humans for high-stakes conversations. Only 9% said they would keep voice AI out of these interactions entirely.


Leaders pointed to consistency and patience as potential advantages. An agent can follow the same process across interactions and deliver required information calmly, even during a tense conversation.


The findings suggest businesses are getting more specific about where voice AI fits, from routine requests to their most sensitive conversations. The nature of each interaction and the level of judgment required now help determine what AI and human agents handle.


## Businesses are building evidence before expanding further


Interest remains high among organizations that haven’t yet deployed agentic voice AI: 44% of non-users are actively planning an investment, and another 42% are considering one.


Competitive pressure and the risk of underinvesting are two of the factors driving that interest. Businesses are also considering the potential consequences of moving too quickly, particularly when deployments directly affect customers or organizational reputation.


For many organizations, pilots and lower-risk use cases provide a way to establish performance before expanding into more complex deployments. Businesses already rolling out voice AI agents follow a similar path, using measured results to decide how far to extend an agent’s responsibilities.


Get[The Rise of Agentic Voice AI: From Conversations to Outcomes](https://www.ringcentral.com/report/2026-agentic-voice-ai-trends.html) for the full findings on how businesses are scaling and evaluating agentic voice AI.


*Source:* *G2 and RingCentral, The Rise of Agentic Voice AI: From Conversations to Outcomes, October 2026. Research based on 359 in-depth interviews with business professionals involved in AI, software, or technology purchasing across healthcare, manufacturing, retail and ecommerce, financial services, transportation, and legal. Participants worked at organizations where voice is an important operational channel and agentic voice AI is being considered, evaluated, piloted, or actively deployed.*


## FAQ


**What is agentic voice AI?**


Agentic voice AI uses AI agents within voice conversations to do more than answer questions. These agents can lead interactions, take action, make decisions within defined areas of responsibility, and capture conversation data that businesses can use to inform future decisions and processes.


**How are businesses using agentic voice AI today?**


Businesses are using voice AI agents for high-volume, repeatable interactions such as customer support and service, scheduling, call routing and intake, reminders, and follow-ups. In the G2 and RingCentral research, 57% of surveyed leaders had voice AI agents actively deployed, with another 10% piloting them.


**What ROI are businesses seeing from agentic voice AI?**


Among leaders with live voice AI deployments who were asked to rate returns, 82% reported positive ROI. They cited benefits including cost savings, time savings, and the ability to redirect employees to more complex work.


**How much autonomy do voice AI agents have?**


Among 191 active deployments in the G2 and RingCentral study, 92% operated with high or partial autonomy. On average, voice AI agents handled 69% of an assigned task without human intervention. Businesses are also establishing conditions for human handoff when agents encounter complexity, uncertainty, or situations requiring additional judgment.


**Can voice AI handle high-stakes conversations?**


Some businesses see a role for voice AI in high-stakes interactions: 35% of leaders surveyed said voice AI can sometimes be a better option than chat-based AI or humans for high-stakes conversations, citing consistency and patience as potential advantages. At the same time, some businesses bring humans in earlier when conversations are emotional, complex, or require significant judgment.


**What are the biggest concerns with agentic voice AI?**


Brand and customer impact is the most commonly cited concern among leaders surveyed. Fifty-nine percent cited potential harm to brands or customers, compared with 24% citing privacy and governance and 17% citing accuracy and reliability. This means businesses are evaluating voice AI on factors beyond accuracy, including resolution, customer feedback, human review, and how agents handle difficult interactions.
